description: The agreement half of the adjacency ruling, for the containers where both spellings are malformed and so cannot be proven as a value, plus the round-2 review finding on the entry lookahead and the regression the ruling's direction had to avoid. A newline separates exactly like a space (`spec/grammar.md:248`), so the newline and spaced spellings of the parenthesized source must produce the SAME diagnostics -- the assertion is that they are malformed in the SAME WAY, not merely that they are malformed. Its execution twin, `core-language/expressions/a-newline-separates-like-a-space`, runs the same shapes in the container where both spellings are well-formed. Both fixtures are regression guards, NOT witnesses: neither could have detected this fix, because the container that exhibited the defect differed only in its AST, and a fixture sees events and diagnostics, never a tree. The comprehension and control rows are the guard: a newline after a header selects the long `... end` body form (`spec/grammar.md:34`), so the `[` binds as a BODY rather than as a selector on the header's last operand, and each raises `ol-missing-end`. A narrowing can only make the `[` LESS likely to bind, so those are strictly more protected than before -- asserted here rather than assumed, and asserted in their SPLIT form, which is the only form that exercises the newline. The dict rows pin `spec/grammar.md:314`: a call still owed an operand is unfinished exactly as an operator is, so the unfinished value's own grammar position wins and no entry opens. Measured at `0277d5ff` before the fix -- and stated for the SPLIT spelling, because an earlier version of this description attributed it to the one-line spelling, which is false -- `{ a: sentence 1` + newline + `mod: 2 }` parsed CLEAN into two entries, `a` and `mod`, leaving `sentence` one argument short, which `check()` then reported as `ol-not-enough-inputs` on a program the grammar says is simply a malformed entry -- as its own `{ a: 1 + b: 2 }` example is. The one-line `{ a: sentence 1 mod: 2 }` behaved correctly at that tip: it raised `ol-bad-token` twice at parse stage, opened no entry keyed `mod`, and so never reached `check()` at all. The newline was the whole of the difference, which is this slice's thesis. Both spellings of each are here because the one-line and multi-line forms must agree; the complete-call counterpart, where the key DOES open its entry, pulls the opposite way and is pinned in `packages/parser/src/newline-continuations-and-delimiters.test.mjs`.
